overview: Mossi political history includes several kingdoms in present-day Burkina Faso. Their populations developed through conquest, migration and incorporation of existing communities. Ouagadougou was influential, but it was not an ancient capital governing every Mossi kingdom.

periods.title: Several kingdoms take shape
periods.summary: Ruling groups from the south established kingdoms among existing populations. The resulting communities included different origins and institutions; their formation was a process, not one dated founding.

periods.title: Conquest and imposed protectorate
periods.summary: French occupation of Ouagadougou and a protectorate treaty altered political authority. Colonial claims of one homogeneous Mossi territory obscured the region’s separate kingdoms.

periods.title: Later evidence of continuing crafts
periods.summary: Surviving twentieth-century pottery and textiles document skilled production. These objects illuminate later Mossi life without establishing that every practice existed unchanged centuries earlier.

items.text: Duperray’s research describes kingdoms formed through encounters between incoming ruling lineages and established populations. Political incorporation did not erase differences of origin. This helps explain why a single map label covers multiple communities and centres of authority.

Yarse communities included Muslim merchants. Oral traditions link many lineages with Mande origins, while others became Yarse through local relationships. Duperray’s interviews reveal changing identities rather than a merchant population with one uniform ancestry.

The protectorate treaty of January 1897 helped France claim a wider territory. Beucher argues that officials enlarged the apparent authority of Ouagadougou’s ruler, the Moogo Naaba, to justify colonial control. The resulting hierarchy cannot simply be projected backward.

A Smithsonian Mossi vessel, made in the middle or late twentieth century, carries impressed patterns below and incised zigzags above. The museum describes pottery used for water, grain, cooking and brewing beer, placing decorated ceramics within ordinary household work.

The Smithsonian’s technique account describes shaping clay over a mould, then adding coils to build the upper vessel. Drying, decoration and firing followed. Millet stalks, wood and manure supplied fuel. Both men and women participated in these pottery traditions.

A late twentieth-century Mossi shawl in the British Museum consists of thirteen narrow cotton strips sewn together. Handspun thread, indigo dye and additional patterned weft at the ends show several kinds of work within one textile.

The museum suggests this cloth may be a diisa prestige shawl, given by a mother to a son on marriage and later used as a burial shroud. That social interpretation is qualified; it is not a securely documented biography of this particular textile.

The High Museum’s karan-wemba figure represents an honoured older woman. Its ridged coiffure and geometric bodily marks connect sculpture with appearance and social status. Patt relates the work to Yatenga traditions while stressing differences among Mossi artistic communities.

Radiocarbon analysis placed the High Museum figure’s wood around the sixteenth century. Wood age does not establish when an artist carved it. Patt considers the possibility of a much later sculpture made from old timber, so an exact early creation date remains unproven.

The PLU collection account describes carving masks from green wood with an adze and knife, then smoothing them with rough leaves. A mask’s performance required further work: fibre fittings, clothing and rattles connected the carved object with a moving, sounding costume.

The same account places cooking, grinding and grain storage within household compounds. These workspaces connect the material arts with food preparation and farming. They describe recorded Mossi settings, not a single house plan shared by every kingdom or historical century.

ending.text: French forces occupied Ouagadougou in September 1896, followed by the 1897 protectorate. Other kingdoms had their own encounters with colonial rule. Royal authority was constrained and reshaped; this political change did not mark the disappearance of Mossi people or their artistic traditions.
